name: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR)

lead: FWHR is the width of the face across the cheekbones divided by the height from upper lip to brow. Looksmaxxing users measure it from photos and treat a wider value as a stronger, more masculine and imposing face, then weigh beards and hairstyles against it.

Researchers have studied it since the late 2000s as a cue of dominance and aggression. A 2015 meta-analysis found the ratio larger in men than women with a small effect (d = 0.11), and another found a small positive link with men's aggression; some studies have not replicated this, and scientific work often links higher values with perceived threat. A study of adolescents found no association with testosterone levels.

paras: People measure FWHR from a straight-on photo and compare it with community targets. They then adjust what they can, such as facial hair, hairstyle and leanness, which change how wide or narrow the face reads.

Measuring is harmless, though camera distance and lens change the measured value. Cosmetic or hormonal approaches to widen the face, including among minors, are medical interventions, and no study shows that treatments change FWHR.

angle.text: Forum users calculate fWHR from photos and treat a higher ratio as a sign of a stronger, more masculine face, then weigh beards and hairstyles against it. Research links it weakly to perceived dominance and aggression.

lead: Facial width-to-height ratio (FWHR or fWHR) is the distance between the cheekbones (bizygomatic width) divided by the height of the upper face, typically measured between the upper lip and the brow.[1][2] It is a size-independent measure and has been studied as a possible sexually dimorphic cue linked to dominance, threat and aggression.[1][2]

A 2015 meta-analysis found the ratio was larger in men than in women, with a small effect size (d = 0.11).[1] A separate 2015 meta-analysis reported a small but significant positive relationship between men's FWHR and aggression.[2] Other work has found the link depends on factors such as income, and some studies have not replicated it.[3]

In looksmaxxing, FWHR became a standard metric. Grokipedia says community sources treat values around 1.8 or above as ideal for masculinity, while noting these are informal standards, and that scientific studies connect higher FWHR with perceived dominance and threat and often lower attractiveness ratings.[4]

paras: Width is taken as the upper bizygomatic width, the widest part of the face across the cheekbones, and height as the distance from roughly the nasion, level with the top of the eyelids, to the top of the upper lip.[5] Some descriptions, including the one used in many forum posts, instead measure from the brow, and different landmark choices give different values.[5] Because the ratio divides one facial dimension by another, it does not depend on overall head size.[1]

Researchers have noted that working from photographs can add error, because facial expressions move the lip and brow landmarks, and that camera focal length alters the depicted shape of a face.[5][6] Forum users report the same effect in practice: the same face can produce noticeably different values from close and distant photographs.

A 2008 study of laboratory aggression tasks and varsity and professional hockey players, by Carre and McCormick, reported that FWHR was associated with aggressive behavior.[7][5] A 2009 paper found that observers could estimate aggression from neutral faces and that their estimates tracked FWHR.[8] A later experiment found that estimates stayed accurate when faces were blurred or cropped, which preserve the ratio, but dropped when faces were scrambled, which disrupts it.[9] A neuroimaging study reported that amygdala reactivity to angry faces was related to aggression only among men with larger FWHR.[10] A 2012 paper linked facial structure with unethical behavior.[11]

Work on social outcomes followed. A 2012 study reported that men with wider faces were more generous to their in-group when out-group competition was salient.[12] A 2015 paper examined bizygomatic width as a cue of formidability.[13] Wikipedia also summarizes studies reporting associations with CEO financial performance (Wong, Ormiston and Haselhuhn, 2011) and with performance among professional basketball players in Japan (Sato and colleagues, 2021), and a primate study linked the ratio to alpha status in capuchin monkeys.[5]

Later work questioned parts of this literature. A 2017 study reported that FWHR did not predict self-reported behavioral tendencies.[14] A 2018 study found FWHR was linked to dominance depending on income and testosterone and noted failures to replicate the aggression link.[3] A 2016 study found FWHR was not associated with adolescent testosterone levels, prompting commentaries and a response.[15] Deaner and colleagues argued in 2012 that body weight rather than FWHR predicted aggression in professional hockey players, and a 2015 study reported no clear sex difference in FWHR in White European faces across photographs, 3D scans and direct measurement.[5] A 2022 direct replication of an earlier study reported that FWHR predicted fighting success.[16] A 2023 study suggested observer bias plays a role: participants asked to draw or edit aggressive-dominant fictitious males produced faces with wider proportions.[17]

A 2014 speed-dating study examined how facial ratios and perceived dominance related to mate choice, and Wikipedia summarizes it as finding that women's attraction to men was tied to FWHR.[18][5] The 2015 meta-analysis found FWHR cued judgements of masculinity in men (r =.35) and was related to body mass index (r =.31).[1] Grokipedia adds that studies often connect higher FWHR with perceived dominance and threat and with lower attractiveness ratings in some contexts, so how a given ratio is received depends on the setting and the observers.[4] A 2018 study also reported that FWHR predicted how much humanity observers ascribed to faces.[19]

Many authors propose that pubertal testosterone shapes craniofacial growth and the link between the ratio and aggression, an idea the neuroimaging study raised.[10] The 2016 adolescent study found no association with testosterone levels, and the 2018 study reported that any testosterone link depended on income.[15][3] The BMI association in the meta-analysis means adiposity in the cheeks can also move the measured width.[1]

No studies found of FWHR in a clinical treatment setting, such as a trial testing an intervention that changes it. The research above is observational and experimental psychology: meta-analyses report a small sex difference and a small association with aggression in men, with mixed replication.[1][2][3]

Focal length affects the depicted shape of faces and how they are perceived.[6] A looksmax.org user reported that his FWHR measured about 1.75 to 1.8 from close range but about 2.0 from a long distance, and another replied that the measure is useful mainly at extremes.

Users post photos for FWHR calculation, debate what counts as high or low and discuss whether bone width can change in puberty. Grokipedia says community sources treat values around 1.8 or above as ideal for masculinity and describes the numeric targets as informal community standards rather than validated criteria.[4]

FWHR sits alongside other framework terms such as the midface ratio, facial thirds and bitemporal width, and users often combine it with jaw and cheekbone assessments when describing an overall facial type.
